extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors and patent attorneys handling USPTO examination and PTAB post-grant proceedings (U.S. obviousness practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for defeating or undermining a USPTO obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) rejection by attacking the examiner’s prima facie case and related legal/record sufficiency issues during prosecution and PTAB proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's initial burden to establish a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO bears the initial burden of factually supporting any prima facie conclusion of obviousness; the examiner must step back in time and into the shoes of the person of ordinary skill in the art when the invention was unknown and just before it was made. See MPEP §2142.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner does not establish a prima facie case, the applicant need not submit rebuttal evidence. Attack the sufficiency of the examiner’s factual support (lack of references, lack of reasoning) to avoid having to rebut and to avoid claim amendments that could create estoppel. Cite MPEP §2142 and pertinent case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — A: combining prior art elements to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is one common rationale for obviousness (MPEP §2143 grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show unpredictability, absence of teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine, or that combination would not yield the claimed result; cite relevant Federal Circuit authority discussed in the Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — B: simple substitution of known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results is a listed rationale for obviousness (MPEP §2143 grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the substitution is not simple or predictable, that critical parameters are different, or that substitution would cause inoperability or loss of function; support with evidence/declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — C: applying a known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods or products) in the same way is another obviousness rationale (MPEP §2143 grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate differences in function, unexpected results, or lack of guidance from the prior art that would lead one to apply the technique in the claimed manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — D: applying a known technique to a device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method or product) that is ready for improvement to yield predictable results is an obviousness rationale (MPEP §2143 grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the prior art did not make the device 'ready for improvement' toward the claimed solution, or that doing so would have been unpredictable or inoperable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — E: 'obvious to try' (finite, predictable solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' applies where choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success would render an invention obvious (KSR and MPEP §2143 discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge by showing the universe of options was not finite, that parameters were unpredictable, or that prior art gave no guidance as to which choices would succeed. Use Eisai, Kubin, Pfizer and KSR lines of authority to frame arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — F: predictable cross-field variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or a different field if those variations are predictable to a person of ordinary skill (MPEP §2143 grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show lack of predictability across fields, differences in problems/solutions, or absence of motivation to adapt the prior art across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales — G: teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention is a common rationale (MPEP §2143(I)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attack the asserted TSM: show no suggestion in the prior art, reliance on applicant’s disclosure (hindsight), or that the asserted motivation is unsupported by record evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusory or unsupported examiner reasoning / reliance on 'common sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's obviousness rejection that is conclusory or relies only on common sense without factual explanation or evidentiary support is insufficient (KSR, In re Lee, In re Zurko, In re Nuvasive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always challenge conclusory rejections; require the examiner to set forth a reasoned explanation supported by the record. Cite the controlling authorities and demand factual support rather than unexplained appeals to 'common knowledge' or 'common sense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to consider the totality of the evidence (including rebuttal evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must consider all evidence of record, including rebuttal evidence submitted during prosecution; decisions must be based on the totality of the record (MPEP §2141(V), §2145; In re Eli Lilly; In re Chu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the examiner failed to weigh applicant-submitted evidence or only considered its 'knockdown' value. Emphasize that rebuttal facts must be evaluated along with earlier facts and that prosecution give-and-take matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete Graham analysis required (four Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness legal conclusion depends on: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) relevant secondary considerations. All four must be analyzed (Graham; KSR; MPEP §2141).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge any faulty or incomplete Graham analysis. Under the first factor, ensure references are analogous art and that issues like enablement, priority date, and the prior art’s entirety are considered. Treat the four factors as non‑alternatives that must be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety (no cherry-picking)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must consider each prior-art reference in its entirety; it is impermissible to pick and choose only the portions that support obviousness while ignoring parts that lead away (In re Wesslau; Bausch & Lomb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out language or sections of cited references that teach away or undermine the examiner’s position; require consideration of the full teaching of a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: Both pre-AIA and post-AIA law requires considering the claimed invention as a whole in the Section 103 inquiry; focusing on an isolated difference may improperly introduce hindsight (MPEP §2141.02; Jones v. Hardy; Princeton Biochemicals; Allergan v. Apotex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the examiner improperly dissected the claim or used the invention as a roadmap; emphasize inherent properties and combination effects that show nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner ignored one or more claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: All claim limitations must be considered when assessing patentability; if a reference does not disclose one or more limitations, a rejection is improper (MPEP §2143.03; Medrad; In re Grasselli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate overlooked limitations, interpret claim language (including function-based interpretations), and show the examiner failed to account for limitations even when §112 or new matter issues were raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the number of predictable solutions was not finite
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge any conclusion that the invention was merely one of a finite number of predictable solutions by demonstrating a wide range of possible outcomes and uncertainties (Eisai; Ortho-McNeil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map out the choices an artisan would have faced and the uncertainties for each choice; show that the prior art universe could not be narrowed to a small, predictable set of candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge the asserted motivation to combine or modify prior art (multiple grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assert that the examiner failed to show a person of ordinary skill would have been reasonably motivated to combine/modify cited prior art; possible sub-grounds include: prior art gave no basis for modification; proposed modification renders art inoperable; prior art did not recognize the problem/solution; prior art teaches away; prosecution history of the cited art rebuts the motivation; examiner mischaracterizes the state of knowledge; no reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific arguments tailored to the ground(s) at issue: (a) show lack of suggestion in prior art; (b) show inoperability or loss of intended function (In re Fritch; In re Ratti; In re Gordon); (c) show the prior art did not recognize the problem or suggest the solution (Cardiac Pacemakers); (d) show teachings away (see standard from Gurley/Fulton/Syntex but note high bar); (e) examine prosecution histories of cited patents/applications for statements or amendments that counsel against the asserted combination (Cohen/Holden example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art teaches away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art reference teaches away when its disclosures are unlikely to produce the objective of the applicant’s invention; mere disclosure of alternatives or a description as somewhat inferior is usually not enough to teach away (In re Gurley; In re Fulton; MPEP §2143(E)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to show that the prior art would have led artisans in a different direction or discouraged the combination claimed. Understand that teaching away is a high bar and requires evidence of discouragement or incompatibility with the invention’s objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reasonable expectation of success — examine conflicts and submit evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires at least a reasonable expectation of success; analyze conflicts among references and consider submitting evidence (declarations, affidavits) showing the prior art did not provide an expectation of success (In re Dow Chem.; In re Rinehart; Amgen v. Chugai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for conflicting teachings among prior art references and highlight them. Prepare and submit declarations or experimental data showing unpredictability or lack of expectation. Be mindful of timing, quality, and the duty of candor when submitting declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriately applied 'obvious to try' — emphasize unpredictability and unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-KSR, 'obvious to try' can support obviousness in certain circumstances (finite predictable options and design pressure), but it is erroneous where the prior art left numerous choices or provided only general guidance (KSR; Kubin; Eisai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge an 'obvious to try' finding by emphasizing that the inventor faced numerous possible choices, critical parameters were unknown, or prior art offered no direction; if possible, show unexpected results to rebut an 'obvious to try' inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of declarations, contacting authors, and prosecution-history evidence to rebut examiner positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tactics include filing declarations about the state of the art, producing authors' retractions or testimony, and using the prosecution history of cited references to rebut asserted motivations or teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: obtain an author retraction (Louvel/Munsat example), prepare expert declarations addressing state of knowledge or unpredictability, and scrutinize cited references' file histories for statements contrary to the examiner’s asserted motivation. Ensure declarations are timely, thorough, and comply with duty of candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution when submitting rebuttal evidence — timing, quality, duty of candor, and estoppel risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting data or declarations may undermine the prima facie case but must be carefully planned; defective declarations can be harmful and may create prosecution history estoppel or duty-of-candor issues (e.g., K-40 IPR example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare high-quality, well-documented declarations and data early enough in prosecution when helpful; avoid inconsistent or non-disclosed data; be mindful that admissions or evidence may be used later against the patentee in IPRs or litigation and could give rise to estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite the MPEP and controlling case law during prosecution (don't leave case law as an afterthought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of nonobviousness should cite the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure and pertinent case law during prosecution so the examiner’s decision reflects those authorities and to preserve arguments for PTAB or court challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include citations in footnotes and argument text. Providing legal authority during prosecution makes the rationale part of the record and avoids later claims that such authorities were afterthoughts.
